hints: Look at the carbon joined to two oxygens in ibuprofen, one as C=O and one as OH, and recall which acid functional group this combination defines.
Look at paracetamol for an OH joined directly to the benzene ring and a nitrogen joined to a C=O, and recall how these two groups are named differently from alcohols and amines.
walkthrough:
Read the oxygen groups in ibuprofen**
Focus on the right hand end, $\text{-C(=O)OH}$. A carbonyl plus a hydroxyl on the same carbon is the classic signature of a carboxylic acid. The benzene ring is already counted, so this is the other group.

Read the two heteroatom groups in paracetamol**
On the right, $\text{-OH}$ is attached directly to the benzene ring. That direct ring to OH link makes it a phenol, not an alcohol. On the left, nitrogen is attached to a $\text{C=O}$, $\text{CH}_3\text{C(=O)NH-}$, which is the signature of an amide.

Final answer: ibuprofen: carboxylic acid (carboxyl group)
paracetamol: phenol and amide

hints: Think about how many groups must be attached to a carbon and how they must differ for mirror images to be non-superimposable.
walkthrough:
Picture why mirror images do not overlap**
Imagine a carbon with four completely different arms. Its mirror image cannot be rotated to match the original, just like left and right hands. If any two arms are the same, you can rotate to match and chirality is lost. So the definition is simply a carbon with four different groups attached.
Final answer: A carbon (atom) bonded to four different atoms or groups.

hints: Locate the chiral carbon in ibuprofen as the carbon joined to the benzene ring, a $\text{CH}_3$ group, a H atom and the $\text{COOH}$ group.
Recall that the two stereoisomers are mirror images, so draw the same connectivity but swap the wedge and dash positions of two groups at that chiral carbon.
walkthrough:
Pinpoint the chiral carbon**
Look along the side chain $\text{Ar-CH(CH}_3\text{)-C(=O)OH}$. That benzylic $\text{CH}$ carbon carries four different groups: the aryl ring, $\text{CH}_3$, H, and $\text{COOH}$. That is your stereocentre.

Draw a mirror pair**
Keep all the rest of the molecule identical. At the chiral carbon, draw one isomer with, for example, $\text{CH}_3$ on a solid wedge and H on a hashed dash, and the second isomer with $\text{CH}_3$ on a hashed dash and H on a solid wedge. The two structures must be non-superimposable mirror images.

Final answer: Two enantiomers of ibuprofen, identical connectivity with opposite 3D arrangement at $\text{Ar-CH(CH}_3\text{)COOH}$ carbon: one with wedge for one substituent and dash for another, the second as the mirror image with wedge and dash reversed.

hints: Recall that $\text{LiAlH}_4$ is a strong reducing agent that converts $\text{COOH}$ to $\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ but leaves a benzene ring untouched.
Recall what $\text{LiAlH}_4$ does to an amide carbonyl, $\text{CH}_3\text{C(=O)NH-}$, and whether a phenol $\text{OH}$ is reduced under these conditions.
walkthrough:
Reduce the acid in ibuprofen**
$\text{LiAlH}_4$ delivers hydride to the carboxyl carbon and removes the C=O oxygen as water on work up. So $\text{-COOH}$ becomes $\text{-CH}_2\text{OH}$. The rest of ibuprofen, including the benzene ring and alkyl side chain, is unchanged.

Reduce the amide in paracetamol**
Paracetamol has no carboxylic acid, but it has an amide. $\text{LiAlH}_4$ strips the carbonyl oxygen from the amide to give an amine. So $\text{CH}_3\text{C(=O)NH-Ar}$ becomes $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{NH-Ar}$. The phenolic $\text{-OH}$ on the ring is not reduced, so it stays as $\text{-OH}$.

Final answer: product with ibuprofen: $\text{Ar-CH(CH}_3\text{)CH}_2\text{OH}$, the carboxylic acid reduced to a primary alcohol.
product with paracetamol: $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{NH-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{-OH}$, the amide $\text{CH}_3\text{CONH-}$ reduced to $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{NH-}$ with phenol unchanged.

hints: Think about which reagent reacts with a carboxylic acid to give effervescence but is too weak a base to react with a phenol.
Think about which reagent decolourises with a phenol by rapid ring substitution but does not react with a benzoic acid type side chain under these conditions.
walkthrough:
Decode reagent D from the table**
D reacts with ibuprofen but not paracetamol. Ibuprofen has $\text{-COOH}$, paracetamol has phenol and amide. A carbonate solution is basic enough to deprotonate a carboxylic acid with $\text{CO}_2$ evolution, but not acidic enough phenol to react significantly. So D fits a carbonate.

Decode reagent E from the table**
E reacts with paracetamol but not ibuprofen. A phenol ring is highly activated toward electrophilic substitution, so bromine water or chlorine is decolourised rapidly to give a white precipitate of brominated phenol. Ibuprofen has a normal benzene ring with no strong activating $\text{-OH}$, so no rapid reaction. So E fits $\text{Br}_2$ or $\text{Cl}_2$.

Final answer: D: $\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3$ or $\text{NaHCO}_3$ or any carbonate / hydrogencarbonate.
E: $\text{Br}_2$ (bromine water) or $\text{Cl}_2$.

hints: Remember that a carboxylic acid plus carbonate gives the carboxylate anion, so replace the acidic $\text{OH}$ proton with $\text{O}^{-}$ paired with $\text{Na}^{+}$.
walkthrough:
Form the salt**
Keep the whole ibuprofen carbon skeleton exactly the same. Simply remove $\text{H}^{+}$ from the $\text{-COOH}$ to leave $\text{-COO}^{-}$, balanced by $\text{Na}^{+}$. No other group changes, and $\text{CO}_2$ and water are the by products.
Final answer: Sodium ibuprofenate: $\text{Ar-CH(CH}_3\text{)COO}^{-}\text{Na}^{+}$, same ibuprofen skeleton with $\text{COOH}$ converted to $\text{COO}^{-}\text{Na}^{+}$.

hints: Visualise the phenol ring with $\text{OH}$ activating ortho positions, noting the para position is already blocked by the amide group.
walkthrough:
Brominate the activated ring**
The $\text{-OH}$ group strongly activates ortho and para positions. In paracetamol the para position carries the $\text{-NHCOCH}_3$ group, so it is blocked. Substitution therefore occurs at the two free ortho positions to the $\text{OH}$, giving the dibromo product. The amide side chain is unchanged.
Final answer: 2,6-dibromoparacetamol: paracetamol ring with Br atoms at both ortho positions to the $\text{OH}$ group, $\text{CH}_3\text{CONH-C}_6\text{H}_2\text{Br}_2\text{-OH}$.

hints: Recall how $\text{AlCl}_3$ accepts $\text{Cl}^{-}$ from an acyl chloride to leave the acylium cation and the tetrachloroaluminate anion.
walkthrough:
Make the real electrophile**
$\text{AlCl}_3$ is an electron pair acceptor. It pulls $\text{Cl}^{-}$ away from $\text{CH}_3\text{COCl}$. That leaves the acylium ion, $\text{CH}_3\text{C}^{+}\text{=O}$, which is the strong electrophile that will attack the ring, plus $\text{AlCl}_4^{-}$.
Final answer: $$\text{CH}_3\text{COCl} + \text{AlCl}_3 \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CO}^{+} + \text{AlCl}_4^{-}$$

hints: Start with the benzene pi electrons of X attacking the $\text{CH}_3\text{CO}^{+}$ carbon, and show this with a curly arrow from the ring to the electrophile.
Recall the shape of the positively charged arenium (Wheland) intermediate with the new $\text{COCH}_3$ group attached and the positive charge delocalised in the ring.
Think about how aromaticity is restored by breaking the C-H bond at the site of attack and returning its electrons into the ring.
walkthrough:
Attack by the ring**
See the benzene in X as a source of pi electrons. Draw a curly arrow from the ring to the carbonyl carbon of $\text{CH}_3\text{CO}^{+}$. The pi bond breaks to form a new C-C bond, and the positive charge moves into the ring.

Draw the intermediate**
You now have a cyclohexadienyl cation. The $\text{COCH}_3$ group and a hydrogen sit on the same $sp^3$ carbon, and the ring carries a delocalised positive charge. This loss of aromaticity makes it high in energy, so it quickly reacts further.

Restore the aromatic ring**
Draw a curly arrow from the C-H bond at the attacked carbon back into the ring. That bond breaks, $\text{H}^{+}$ leaves, and the pi system reforms. The product is the para acylated ring Y, with full aromaticity restored.

Final answer: Curly arrow from benzene pi system of X to C of $\text{CH}_3\text{CO}^{+}$; arenium intermediate with $\text{COCH}_3$ attached, H still attached, positive charge delocalised in ring; curly arrow from C-H bond back into ring to restore aromaticity giving Y plus $\text{H}^{+}$.

hints: Combine the role of the positive acylium electrophile with the fact that a hydrogen on the benzene ring is replaced while aromaticity is retained.
walkthrough:
Name the pattern**
A positive electrophile attacks the electron rich ring and substitutes for hydrogen without destroying the benzene system. That is the classic electrophilic substitution pathway.
Final answer: Electrophilic substitution (electrophilic aromatic substitution).
